Pre-requisite: Concept of Differentiation and Integration.

Course Objective

This course is aimed to teach the drawbacks of classical physics in explaining several experimental
observations and old quantum theory; and to discuss the necessity of new mechanics and the laws related to
it and their applications. This course also endeavors to make students understand the phenomenon of
thermodynamics and mathematical framework and laws of statistical mechanics, along with their possible
applications.

Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to-
1. Explain the basic laws related to quantum mechanics and apply them to solve related problems
2. Elucidate the concepts of statistical mechanics and solve problems using the same
3. Apply the concepts of statistical physics and thermodynamics to excel in their study of complex
engineering systems

Detailed Syllabus

Unit | Description Duration

1. | Introduction to Quantum Physics
Black body radiation, Explanation of it using the photon concept, Photoelectric effect,
Compton effect, de Broglie hypothesis, Experiments demonstrating wave properties of 09
electron: Electron interference (double slit experiment), Electron Diffraction (Davison -
Germer experiment), Uncertainty Principle. Wave-particle duality, Born’s interpretation
of the wave function, Verification of matter waves, Uncertainty principle.

2. | Basic Postulates of Quantum Mechanics
Concept of wave function, Superposition principle of eigenstates. Concept of collapse of

wave function. Time dependent and time independent Schrodinger Equation, Concept 09
of free particle, particle in an infinite and finite potential well.

3. | Concept of Quantum Tunnelling
Reflection and Transmission coefficients. Few realistic examples of tunnelling, e.g., alpha 09

decay, Probe microscopes (Scanning Tunnelling microscope). Simple Harmonic
Oscillator, explanation in 1D (no detailed derivation).

Boltzmann) and Quantum statistics, [Bose Einstein (BE) and Fermi Dirac (FD)]. 10
Derivation of classical statistics and BE and FD statistics. Equipartition of energy,
Planck’s distribution.

5. | Thermodynamics
Zeroth law of thermodynamics, first law of thermodynamics, brief discussion on

application of 1st law, second law of thermodynamics and concept of Engine, entropy, 08

Pre-requisite: Knowledge of fundamental concepts in Algebra, Differential

Course Objective
This course aims to instil in prospective engineer’s knowledge of concepts and techniques
in Linear Algebra and Differential Equations. It also prepares the students to deal with
advanced level of Mathematics and applications that would be essential for their disciplines.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to-
1. Understand the fundamental concepts of linear algebra, including vector spaces, subspaces,
basis, and dimension, and apply them to solve problems related to linear independence and
dependence.
2. Analyze and apply linear transformations, eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and diagonalization
techniques, including the Rank-Nullity Theorem and the Cayley-Hamilton Theorem, to
solve problems involving matrices.
3. Solve first-order ordinary differential equations using exact equations, integrating factors,
and special methods such as Bernoulli’s equation and orthogonal trajectories.
4. Formulate and solve higher-order linear differential equations using methods such as the
operator method, undetermined coefficients, variation of parameters, and power series
solutions, including Legendre and Bessel equations.
5. Understand the formation and classification of partial differential equations and apply direct
integration and separation of variables techniques to solve them in Cartesian coordinates.
6. Apply concepts from linear algebra and differential equations to model and solve real-world
problems in engineering, physics, and applied sciences.

Course Objective
The minor project is designed to bridge the gap between theory and practice.   It provides an
opportunity to students to explore various societal problems and provide innovative solutions for
the same. The course encourage students to develop technical and soft skills. The students may
also work in interdisciplinary areas which will help broaden their scope and learning in different
domains.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Identify, analyze and solve problems creatively using critical and design thinking principles.
2. Implement the prototype/proof of concept using fundamental and disciplinary concepts and
methods.
3. Manage a team project.

Syllabus
A student group is required to identify some real world problem and develop a solution using
design and critical thinking principles. They may develop a working model or a proof of concept
of the solution. At the end of the semester, students will submit a report detailing the problem
analysis process and designed solution. Each group will present their work before examiners.

Course Objective

This course is aimed to teach the drawbacks of classical physics in explaining several experimental
observations and old quantum theory; and to discuss the necessity of new mechanics and the laws related to
it and their applications. This course also endeavors to make students understand the phenomenon of
thermodynamics and mathematical framework and laws of statistical mechanics, along with their possible
applications.

Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to-
1. Explain the basic laws related to quantum mechanics and apply them to solve related problems
2. Elucidate the concepts of statistical mechanics and solve problems using the same
3. Apply the concepts of statistical physics and thermodynamics to excel in their study of complex
engineering systems

Detailed Syllabus

Unit | Description Duration

1. | Introduction to Quantum Physics
Black body radiation, Explanation of it using the photon concept, Photoelectric effect,
Compton effect, de Broglie hypothesis, Experiments demonstrating wave properties of 09
electron: Electron interference (double slit experiment), Electron Diffraction (Davison -
Germer experiment), Uncertainty Principle. Wave-particle duality, Born’s interpretation
of the wave function, Verification of matter waves, Uncertainty principle.

2. | Basic Postulates of Quantum Mechanics
Concept of wave function, Superposition principle of eigenstates. Concept of collapse of

wave function. Time dependent and time independent Schrodinger Equation, Concept 09
of free particle, particle in an infinite and finite potential well.

3. | Concept of Quantum Tunnelling
Reflection and Transmission coefficients. Few realistic examples of tunnelling, e.g., alpha 09

decay, Probe microscopes (Scanning Tunnelling microscope). Simple Harmonic
Oscillator, explanation in 1D (no detailed derivation).

Course Objective
The course provide basic orientation towards microeconomic principles and help them understand the
functions of management. This course also aims to understand issues dealing with small-scale economic
phenomena and concepts such as prices and output of firms, industries and resource owners along with
examining market impact of technological change with regards to understand broader aspects of the
economy and its environment.

including scarcity of resources, economic systems, and demand-supply analysis. (K1, K2)

theories to understand consumer decision-making and cost structures in different market
conditions (K2, K3)

price and output determination. (K2, K3)

management functions such as planning, organizing, decision-making, and leadership
based on classical and modern theories. (K2, K3)
5. Understand the Role of Business Functions in Organizational Success - Examine the
significance of key business functions such as finance, marketing, human resources, and
operations, and their interdependence in achieving organizational objectives. (K1, K2)

simplex iterations. Sensitivity analysis. Duality – formulation,
results, dual-simplex and primal-dual algorithms.

applications.

Course Objective
This course is aimed to teach the drawbacks of classical physics in explaining several experimental
observations and old quantum theory; and to discuss the necessity of new mechanics and the laws related to
it and their applications. This course also endeavors to make students understand the phenomenon of
thermodynamics and mathematical framework and laws of statistical mechanics, along with their possible
applications.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to-
1. Interpret the basic laws related to quantum mechanics and apply them to solve related problems
2.   Illustrate the concepts of statistical mechanics and solve problems using the same
3. Apply the concepts of statistical physics and thermodynamics to excel in their study of complex
engineering systems
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Introduction to Quantum Physics
Black body radiation, Explanation of it using the photon concept, Photoelectric effect,
Compton effect, de Broglie hypothesis, Experiments demonstrating wave properties of   09
electron: Electron interference (double slit experiment), Electron Diffraction (Davison -
Germer experiment), Uncertainty Principle. Wave-particle duality, Born’s interpretation
of the wave function, Verification of matter waves, Uncertainty principle.
2.   Basic Postulates of Quantum Mechanics
Concept of wave function, Superposition principle of eigenstates. Concept of collapse of
09
wave function. Time dependent and time independent Schrodinger Equation, Concept
of free particle, particle in an infinite and finite potential well.
3.   Concept of Quantum Tunnelling
Reflection and Transmission coefficients. Few realistic examples of tunnelling, e.g., alpha
09
decay, Probe microscopes (Scanning Tunnelling microscope). Simple Harmonic
Oscillator, explanation in 1D (no detailed derivation).
4.   Introduction to Statistical Physics and its Application
Ensembles (Canonical, Micro canonical and Grand canonical) Classical (Maxwell-
Boltzmann) and Quantum statistics, [Bose Einstein (BE) and Fermi Dirac (FD)].   10
Derivation of classical statistics and BE and FD statistics. Equipartition of energy,
Planck’s distribution.

Course Objective

The principal objective of this course is to provide a basic understanding of biological mechanisms of living
organisms from the perspective of engineers. To encourage engineering students to think about solving
biological problems with engineering tools. To make them aware of the application of engineering principles
in biology and engineering robust solutions inspired by biological examples.

Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. convey that all forms of life have the same building blocks and yet the manifestations are diverse
2. identify and classify microorganisms while understanding molecular basis of DNA as a genetic
material for information transfer
3. classify enzymes and distinguish between different mechanisms of enzyme action

Unit Description Duration

Convey that Biology is as important a scientific discipline as Mathematics, Physics
and Chemistry Bring out the fundamental differences between science and
engineering by drawing a comparison between eye and camera, Bird flying and
aircraft. Mention the most exciting aspect of biology as an independent scientific
discipline. Why we need to study biology? Discuss how biological observations of
18th Century that lead to major discoveries. Examples from -Brownian motion and
the origin of thermodynamics by referring to the original observation of Robert
Brown and Julius Mayor. These examples will highlight the fundamental
importance of observations in any scientific inquiry.

Course Objective

This course aims to instill in students a sound knowledge of probability theory and statistical
techniques. It equips the students with intermediate to advanced level concepts and tools in probability
and statistics that help them tackle relevant problems within engineering domain.

Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Solve problems involving random variables, probability distributions and testing of
hypothesis, correlation and regression
2. Identify suitable probability distribution and testing techniques to solve related problems
3. Apply knowledge of random variables, probability distributions, measures of central tendency,
correlation and regression to solve real life problems
4. Analyse data samples using statistical methods

understanding of mathematical proofs and common mathematical arguments. It will instil
sound knowledge of different topics of discrete mathematics which students will readily apply
in the subsequent courses of their programme.

1. Define and relate basic notions of discrete mathematics
2. Demonstrate the ability to understand mathematical logic, concepts in abstract algebra

and mathematical proof techniques

3. Solve problems based on combinatorics, graph theory and abstract algebra
4.Demonstrate understanding of the applications of algebra, combinatorics and graph
theory

Course Objective
The course provide basic orientation towards microeconomic principles and help them understand the
functions of management. This course also aims to understand issues dealing with small-scale economic
phenomena and concepts such as prices and output of firms, industries and resource owners along with
examining market impact of technological change with regards to understand broader aspects of the
economy and its environment.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Illustrate basic concepts of economics (demand, supply, elasticity, scarcity) and explain
behaviour on individual, households and firm and handle economic data and write economic
report,
2. Analyse and evaluate the impact of Economic Policies and its implication on the Business
Environment,
3. Demonstrate and determine the students towards basic management principles and act as
foundation for higher levels of learning and to be able to handle basic functions of management
(planning, organizing, coordination, and control).

This course provides the fundamental knowledge of computer networks through understanding each
layer of computer network architecture, and transmission systems to network applications. It also
focuses on congestion control techniques, protocols, and application layer functions.

Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Explain the concepts of computer networks, topologies and data communication
2. Analyze the various error detection and correction and medium access techniques
3. Apply network layer addressing and routing techniques to different network topologies
4. Analyze the different protocols of the layered architecture of computer networks

Course Objective
The course aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of Robotic Process Automation (RPA) by
covering its foundational concepts and advanced applications. Students will gain insight into the
historical development and evolution of RPA, along with a deep appreciation for the benefits and
challenges of its implementation. By delving into RPA tools and their features, students will learn to
harness workflow automation, create apps, grasp the distinctions between attended and unattended
bots, and comprehend the symbiotic relationship between RPA and Artificial Intelligence (AI).
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Demonstrate understanding of fundamental RPA concepts, historical evolution, benefits and
process analysis and selection
2. Analyze RPA tools, design bot workflows, and apply decision-making strategies, constructing
optimized automation processes
3. Create user-centric app interfaces, develop integrated app functionalities aligned with RPA
workflows, and deploy applications within operational frameworks
4. Evaluate ethical considerations, including data security and privacy, ensuring compliant RPA
implementations, and making informed decisions regarding automation practices
5. Synthesize software bots for operational process automation of practical importance

Course Objective
The capstone project is designed to provide a culminating design experience to the final-year
students’ learning with essentially required hands-on experience to ensure that they graduate
with the required practical and soft skills. The course aims to encourage students to think
critically, solve challenging problems, do a feasibility study and develop written and oral
communication skills, teamwork and planning. The students may also work in interdisciplinary
areas which will help broaden their scope and learning in different domains.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Select an appropriate problem statement after reviewing the literature and identifying the
research gaps.
2. Formulate the different use cases/feasible design model.
3. Implement the prototype/proof of concept, test and validate the results.
4. Manage a team project.
5. Summarize the topic into a technical report.
Syllabus
A student is required to carry out elaborated project work. The project may be either design
and fabrication work or a simulation and synthesis of a problem/system, and develop
algorithms and verify feasibility of implementation. At the end of the semester students will be
required to submit a report detailing the literature review, design problem formulation,
analysis functional simulation and synthesis, work plan and work done and present his/her
work carried out before examiners.

Objectives:
The objective of this course is to familiarize students with the principles of basic mathematics as
well as to develop an analytical and systematic approach towards solving problems and learn to
apply the concepts in related technology problems.
Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students will be able to
1. Recognize series to obtain solutions for finite and infinite series expansion,
2. Apply vectors to solve related application problems,
3. Find area and volume by using integration techniques,
4. Use derivatives to solve problems and identify ways to express partial derivatives.
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Series
Arithmetic Progression: Definition, nth term, arithmetic mean.
Geometric progression: Definition, nth term, sum of first terms, sum to   8
infinity of a G.P, geometric mean.
Special series: Introduction, exponential series, logarithmic series.
2.   Vector Algebra
Scalar product of two vectors: Geometrical meaning, work done as a scalar
product.
Vector product of two vectors: Geometrical meaning, moment of a force.   10
Product of three and four vectors: Geometrical interpretation, scalar product of
three vectors, vector triple product, scalar and vector product of four vectors,
coplanarity of three vectors, volume of parallelopiped and volume of
tetrahedron.
3.   Integral Calculus
Integration: Method of substitution, integration by partial fractions, special
integrals.   10
Definite integrals: Evaluation of definite integral, theorems on definite integrals,
reduction formulae for sin n x and cos n x (only results).

inverse trigonometric functions, successive differentiation up to second order.
Homogeneous differential equations: First order first degree ordinary   10
differential equations reducible to homogeneous form.
Applications: Rate of change of quantities, tangents and normal, applications of
first order first degree differential equations – population growth, radioactive
decay, LCR circuit, Newton’s law of cooling.

derivatives, Euler's theorem on homogeneous functions, partial differentiation
of implicit functions, total differentiation.

Objectives:
This course is aimed to teach the drawbacks of classical physics in explaining several experimental
observations and old quantum theory; and to discuss the necessity of new mechanics, laws of
thermodynamics and acoustics for engineers.
Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to:
1. understand the physics of acoustics.
2. explain the basic laws related to quantum mechanics and application.
3. elucidate the concepts of statistical mechanics and solve problems using the same.
4. Describe the concepts of thermodynamics and its application.
Detailed Syllabus: ( per session plan )
Unit   Description   Duration
1. Introduction to Acoustic   6
Sound, Intensity of sound, threshold of hearing, loudness of sound, Reverberation
time, sound absorption, Sabines’s formula for reverberation time, determination of
absorption coefficient, Acoustic of building.
2. Basic postulates of quantum mechanics   10
Introduction wave particle duality, Concept of wave function, Superposition
principle of eigenstates. Concept of collapse of wave function. Time dependent and
time independent Schrodinger Equation, Concept of free particle, particle in an
infinite and finite potential well.
3. Concept of Quantum Tunnelling   8
Reflection and Transmission coefficients. Few realistic examples of tunnelling, e.g.,
alpha decay, Probe microscopes (Scanning Tunnelling microscope). Simple
Harmonic Oscillator, explanation in 1D (no detailed derivation). Hydrogen atom.
4. Introduction to Statistical Physics   8
Ensembles (Canonical, Micro canonical and Grand canonical) Classical (Maxwell-
Boltzmann) and Quantum statistics, [Bose Einstein (BE) and Fermi Dirac (FD)].
Introduction to classical statistics and BE and FD statistics.
5.   Applications of Statistical physics   5
Equipartition of energy, Planck’s distribution, Bose-Einstein Condensation

Introduction, microscopic and macroscopic views, thermal equilibrium, Zeroth
law of thermodynamics, temperature, temperature measurement, first law of   8
thermodynamics, second law of thermodynamics and third law   of
thermodynamics and its applications.

the Constitution,

additional powers the bestowed upon the Government at times of Emergency and to
understand the Amendment procedure.

Course Objective
The principal objective of this course is to provide a basic understanding of biological mechanisms
of living organisms from the perspective of engineers. To encourage engineering students to think
about solving biological problems with engineering tools. To make them aware of the application
of engineering principles in biology and engineering robust solutions inspired by biological
examples.
Course Outcomes
After successful completion of the course, student will be able to-
1. convey that all forms of life have the same building blocks and yet the manifestations are
diverse
2. identify and classify microorganisms while understanding molecular basis of DNA as a
genetic material for information transfer
3. classify enzymes and distinguish between different mechanisms of enzyme action
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   3
Introduction
Convey that Biology is as important a scientific discipline as Mathematics,
Physics and Chemistry Bring out the fundamental differences between science
and engineering by drawing a comparison between eye and camera, Bird flying
and aircraft. Mention the most exciting aspect of biology as an independent
scientific discipline. Why we need to study biology? Discuss how biological
observations of 18th Century that lead to major discoveries. Examples from -
Brownian motion and the origin of thermodynamics by referring to the original
observation of Robert Brown and Julius Mayor. These examples will highlight
the fundamental importance of observations in any scientific inquiry.

2.   Classification
Convey that classification per se is not what biology is all about.   6
The underlying   criterion, such   as   morphological,   biochemical   or
ecological   be   highlighted. Hierarchy   of   life   forms at
phenomenological   level. A common thread weaves   this hierarchy
Classification.Discuss classification based on   (a)   cellularity-Unicellular
or multicellular (b) ultrastructure- prokaryotes or eucaryotes. (c) energy and
Carbon utilization -Autotrophs, heterotrophs, lithotropes (d) Ammonia
excretion - aminotelic, uricoteliec, ureotelic (e) Habitata- acquatic or terrestrial
(e) Molecular taxonomy- three major kingdoms of life. A given organism can
come under different category based on classification. Model organisms for the
study of biology come from different groups. E.coli, S.cerevisiae, D.
Melanogaster, C. elegance, A. Thaliana, M. musculus
3.   Genetics
Convey that "Genetics is to biology what Newton's laws are to Physical Sciences"   6
Mendel's laws, Concept of segregation and independent assortment. Concept of
allele. Gene mapping, Gene interaction, Epistasis. Meiosis and Mitosis be taught
as a part of genetics. Emphasis to be give not to the mechanics of cell division
nor the phases but how genetic material passes from parent to offspring.
Concepts of recessiveness and dominance. Concept of mapping of phenotype to
genes. Discuss about the single gene disorders in humans. Discuss the concept
of complementation using human genetics.
4.   Biomolecules   5
Convey that all forms of life has the same building blocks and yet the
manifestations are as diverse as one can imagine Molecules of life. In this context
discuss monomeric units and polymeric structures. Discuss about sugars, starch
and cellulose. Amino acids and proteins. Nucleotides and DNA/RNA. Two
carbon units and lipids.
5.   Enzymes   5
Convey that without catalysis life would not have existed on earth Enzymology:
How to monitor enzyme catalyzed reactions. How does an enzyme catalyze
reactions. Enzyme classification. Mechanism of enzyme action. Discuss at least
two examples. Enzyme kinetics and kinetic- parameters. Why should we know
these parameters to understand biology? RNA catalysis.

6.   Information Transfer   6
The molecular basis of coding and decoding genetic information is universal
Molecular basis of information transfer. DNA as a genetic material. Hierarchy
of DNA structure- from single stranded to double helix to nucleosomes. Concept
of genetic code. Universality and degeneracy of genetic code. Define gene in
terms of complementation and recombination.
7.   Macromolecular analysis   5
How to analyses biological processes at the reductionistic level Proteins-
structure and function. Hierarch in protein structure. Primary secondary,
tertiary and quaternary structure. Proteins as enzymes, transporters, receptors
and structural elements.
8.   Metabolism   5
The fundamental principles of energy transactions are the same in physical and
biological world. Thermodynamics as applied to biological systems. Exothermic
and endothermic versus endergonic and exergonic reactions. Concept of Keq
and its relation to standard free energy. Spontaneity. ATP as an energy currency.
This should include the breakdown of glucose to CO2 + H2O (Glycolysis and
Krebs cycle) and synthesis of glucose from CO2 and H2O (Photosynthesis).
Energy yielding and energy consuming reactions. Concept of Energy Charge.
9.   Microbiology   4
Concept of single celled organisms. Concept of species and strains. Identification
and classification of microorganisms. Microscopy. Ecological aspects of single
celled organisms. Sterilization and media compositions. Growth kinetics.

Course Objective
The course aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of Robotic Process Automation (RPA) by
covering its foundational concepts and advanced applications. Students will gain insight into the
historical development and evolution of RPA, along with a deep appreciation for the benefits and
challenges of its implementation. By delving into RPA tools and their features, students will learn to
harness workflow automation, create apps, grasp the distinctions between attended and unattended
bots, and comprehend the symbiotic relationship between RPA and Artificial Intelligence (AI).
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Demonstrate understanding of fundamental RPA concepts, historical evolution, benefits and
process analysis and selection
2. Analyze RPA tools, design bot workflows, and apply decision-making strategies, constructing
optimized automation processes
3. Create user-centric app interfaces, develop integrated app functionalities aligned with RPA
workflows, and deploy applications within operational frameworks
4. Evaluate ethical considerations, including data security and privacy, ensuring compliant RPA
implementations, and making informed decisions regarding automation practices
5. Synthesize software bots for operational process automation of practical importance

Pre-requisite: Knowledge of all core and elective courses completed till 3rd year.
Course Objective
The capstone project is designed to provide a culminating design experience to the final-year
students’ learning with essentially required hands-on experience to ensure that they graduate
with the required practical and soft skills. The course aims to encourage students to think
critically, solve challenging problems, do a feasibility study and develop written and oral
communication skills, teamwork and planning. The students may also work in interdisciplinary
areas which will help broaden their scope and learning in different domains.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Select an appropriate problem statement after reviewing the literature and identifying the
research gaps.
2. Formulate the different use cases/feasible design model.
3. Implement the prototype/proof of concept, test and validate the results.
4. Manage a team project.
5. Summarize the topic into a technical report.
Syllabus
A student is required to carry out elaborated project work. The project may be either design
and fabrication work or a simulation and synthesis of a problem/system, and develop
algorithms and verify feasibility of implementation. At the end of the semester students will be
required to submit a report detailing the literature review, design problem formulation,
analysis functional simulation and synthesis, work plan and work done and present his/her
work carried out before examiners.

Pre-requisite: Basic proving techniques, concepts of number theory, algebra, pre-
calculus.
Objectives:
1. Train the students in the construction and understanding of mathematical
proofs, exercise common mathematical arguments and proof strategies.
2. Prepare the students to use the basic methods of discrete mathematics in the
subsequent courses of computer science in the design and analysis of algorithms
and software engineering.
Outcomes: After completion of the course, students would be able to:
1. Define and relate basic notions of Graph theory, set theory and relation.
2. Demonstrate the ability to express a logical sentence in terms of predicates,
quantifiers, logical connectives and solve problems using Pigeonhole principle.
3. Solve Problems based on Graphs, groups, rings, relations and their properties.
4. Derive the solution using deductive logic, mathematical induction and basic
counting techniques for a given problem.

Operations and Laws of Sets, Size of a Set, Finite and infinite Sets,
Countable and uncountable Sets, Cartesian Products, Principle of
inclusion and exclusion, Binary Relation, Equivalence Relation, Partial
Ordering Relation.
2   Principles of Mathematical Induction and Basic Counting   8
techniques:
Mathematical Induction, The Well-Ordering Principle, Recursive
definition, The Division algorithm: Prime Numbers, The Greatest
Common Divisor: Euclidean Algorithm, The Fundamental Theorem of
Arithmetic, pigeon-hole principle, permutation, combination.

Course Objective
The course aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of Robotic Process Automation (RPA) by
covering its foundational concepts and advanced applications. Students will gain insight into the
historical development and evolution of RPA, along with a deep appreciation for the benefits and
challenges of its implementation. By delving into RPA tools and their features, students will learn to
harness workflow automation, create apps, grasp the distinctions between attended and unattended
bots, and comprehend the symbiotic relationship between RPA and Artificial Intelligence (AI).

1. Demonstrate understanding of fundamental RPA concepts, historical evolution, benefits and
process analysis and selection
2. Analyze RPA tools, design bot workflows, and apply decision-making strategies, constructing
optimized automation processes
3. Create user-centric app interfaces, develop integrated app functionalities aligned with RPA
workflows, and deploy applications within operational frameworks

implementations, and making informed decisions regarding automation practices.

Pre-requisite: Knowledge of all core and elective courses completed till 3rd year.
Course Objective
The capstone project is designed to provide a culminating design experience to the final-year students’
learning with essentially required hands-on experience to ensure that they graduate with the required
practical and soft skills. The course aims to encourage students to think critically, solve challenging
problems, do a feasibility study and develop written and oral communication skills, teamwork and
planning. The students may also work in interdisciplinary areas which will help broaden their scope and
learning in different domains.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Select an appropriate problem statement after reviewing the literature and identifying the research
gaps.
2. Formulate the different use cases/feasible design model.
3. Implement the prototype/proof of concept, test and validate the results.
4. Manage a team project.
5. Summarize the topic into a technical report.
Syllabus
A student is required to carry out elaborated project work. The project may be either design and
fabrication work or a simulation and synthesis of a problem/system, and develop algorithms and
verify feasibility of implementation. At the end of the semester students will be required to submit a
report detailing the literature review, design problem formulation, analysis functional simulation and
synthesis, work plan and work done and present his/her work carried out before examiners.

Course Objective
The course aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of Robotic Process Automation (RPA) by
covering its foundational concepts and advanced applications. Students will gain insight into the
historical development and evolution of RPA, along with a deep appreciation for the benefits and
challenges of its implementation. By delving into RPA tools and their features, students will learn to
harness workflow automation, create apps, grasp the distinctions between attended and unattended
bots, and comprehend the symbiotic relationship between RPA and Artificial Intelligence (AI).
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Demonstrate understanding of fundamental RPA concepts, historical evolution, benefits and
process analysis and selection
2. Analyze RPA tools, design bot workflows, and apply decision-making strategies, constructing
optimized automation processes
3. Create user-centric app interfaces, develop integrated app functionalities aligned with RPA
workflows, and deploy applications within operational frameworks
4. Evaluate ethical considerations, including data security and privacy, ensuring compliant RPA
implementations, and making informed decisions regarding automation practices.

Course Objective
The objective of this course is to introduce students to the foundational concepts and practices of data
wrangling and enable them to understand how raw data is systematically represented, transformed,
cleaned, explored, and validated for analytical use. The course aims to develop strong data-handling
skills by combining structured data manipulation with visual understanding and ethical, reproducible
data practices.

1. Explain fundamental data structures and data operations used for representing and
manipulating structured data (K1)

workflows (K2)
3. Apply exploratory and applied data wrangling techniques, including categorical handling and
visual data understanding, to analyze datasets (K3)
4. Analyze datasets to ensure data quality, ethical handling, and reproducibility in data
preparation processes (K4)

Course Objective
Students will be familiar with basic rules of probability and will be able to use them in modelling
uncertainty in obtaining and recording data. They will be able to utilize graphical and numerical
summaries of data in understanding data generating processes. To enable the students to analyze data
more effectively using statistical software.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Classify, organize, summarize and visually represent qualitative and quantitative data using
appropriate tabulation and descriptive statistical tools and graphical techniques.( L1 –
Remembering , L2 – Understanding and L3 – Applying)
2. Measure, interpret and analyze variability, skewness, kurtosis, covariance and correlations, and
appropriately visualize relationships in data. (L3 – Applying and L4 – Analyzing)
3. Apply and evaluate concepts of probability, conditional probability, independence, Bayes’
theorem, and compute probabilities using common discrete and continuous distributions.( L3 –
Applying, L4 – Analyzing and L5 – Evaluating)
4. Apply the concepts of discrete and continuous random variables to model uncertainty by defining
probability distributions (PMF, PDF, CDF), computing expected value and variance, and analyzing
joint and marginal distributions of single and two-dimensional random variables. (L3 – Applying,
L4 – Analyzing)
5. Formulate statistical inferences by designing hypothesis tests to validate assumptions and draw
conclusions from sample data.( L6 – Create)

Course Objective
This course aims to introduce students to the fundamental concepts of data and signal analysis. It
provides a strong mathematical foundation for signal representation, processing, and transformation
techniques. The course will help students understand signal characterization, and frequency-domain
analysis using various transforms. Additionally, students will learn the importance of sampling and its
role in digital signal processing, along with Fourier and Laplace transformations for analysing signals in
different domains.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Describe the fundamental concepts of data communication and perform mathematical operations
on signals (K1)
2. Explain convolution techniques & Z-transforms and apply them in analysing discrete-time signals
(K2)
3. Apply the Nyquist Sampling Theorem to determine the optimal sampling rate (K3)
4. Analyse signals using series and transforms to interpret and solve signal processing problems
(K3)

Pre-requisite: Data Wrangling/Data Wrangling Fundamentals and Practices
Course Objective
The objective of this course is to introduce students to the fundamental concepts of data engineering.
The course provides a conceptual understanding of data systems, data architecture, data movement,
data preparation, and basic data pipeline concepts using structured datasets. Emphasis is placed on
understanding how data flows through different stages in a data system, ensuring data quality and
consistency.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to-
1. Explain the structure and components of data systems and basic architectural concepts used in
data-driven applications (K1)
2. Describe different data sources and ingestion mechanisms involved in moving data into a data
system (K2)
3. Apply data structuring and preparation techniques to organize datasets for processing across
multiple stages (K3)
4. Analyze datasets to ensure data quality, consistency, and reliability during data preparation and
integration (K4)

Overview of Data Systems and Architectural Concepts
Role of data engineering in data systems, Difference between data analysis and data   03
1.   engineering, Types of data, Introduction to data architecture, Components of a basic
data system, Conceptual view of data flow in applications, Medallion, Snowflake,
Data Mesh
Data Sources and Ingestion Mechanisms
Understanding data sources, Introduction to data ingestion, Batch data ingestion   03
2.
concepts, Movement of data from source to processing, Organizing ingestion steps

Course Objective
The course would enable students to get a brief introduction of the Indian Constitution and its principles.
The students would have knowledge of concept of ‘State’ and interdependencies of its institutions vis a
vis their relation with fundamental rights.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to-
1. Understand the historic evolution of the Indian Constitution, its drafting, nature and to
understand the principles mentioned in its Preamble
2. Inculcate fundamental rights in its true sense and also the permissible restrictions upon it so as to
enjoy these rights within permissible limits while simultaneously performing their duties and to
apply these principles into their professional lives
3. Ingrain the structure of our polity and role of Judiciary in maintaining the basic structure of the
Constitution
4. Attain knowledge of the Emergency provisions, when and how it is imposed, to know the
additional powers the bestowed upon the Government at times of Emergency and to understand
the Amendment procedure
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration

based on classical and modern theories. (K2, K3)

Pre-requisite: Managing Uncertainty (SEM - III)
Course Objective
This course aims at giving the foundation knowledge Statistical Inference and regression analysis.
In particular, it gives details of theory of Estimation and testing of hypothesis. Both theoretical
aspect will be discussed and practical problems will be dealt with in great detail. In this course
the students also learn different models for categorical data such as Generalized Linear, logit,
logistic and log linear models
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Recall fundamental concepts of confidence intervals, hypothesis testing, and maximum
likelihood estimation (MLE) (L1- Remembering)
2. Explain the likelihood function, maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) across various
distributions (Binomial, Multinomial, Gaussian), and apply the continuous version of
Bayes' theorem. (L2 -Understanding and L3- Applying)
3. Perform hypothesis testing using Z-tests, t-tests, and Chi-square tests for independence
and goodness of fit, including interpretation of p-values, Type I and Type II errors. (L3-
Applying and L4 – Analyzing)
4. Interpret generalized linear models (GLMs) such as logistic regression for binary outcomes,
including log-odds interpretation and model diagnostics. (L2-Understanding)
5. Perform and interpret Ridge and Lasso regression for feature selection with Python
implementations and visualizations (L4-Analyzing)
6. Evaluate and create advanced statistical models, including logistic regression for binary
outcomes and non-parametric tests (Sign Test, Rank Sum Test, Kruskal-Wallis, Friedman
tests), with Python implementations and visualizations. (L5 – Evaluating and L6-Creating)

Course Objective
This course provides an introduction to time series analysis. It will educate students on how to choose an
appropriate forecasting method in a particular environment and then apply it using necessary computations.
It aims to equip students with various forecasting techniques and knowledge on modern statistical methods
for analyzing time series data. It will also provide directions to Improve forecasting using better statistical
models based on statistical analysis
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to –

autocorrelation, and visualize them using various plotting techniques.

diagnostics to identify appropriate forecasting models.

reconciliation methods and compare with alternative approaches.
5. Design advanced forecasting solutions using complex seasonality, the Prophet model, VARs,
bootstrapping, and bagging on real-world datasets using statistical software.

of elements, mole concept, and basic organic chemistry & to familiarize with the concepts and

Pre-requisite: Concept of Differentiation and Integration.
Course Objective
This course is aimed to teach the drawbacks of classical physics in explaining several experimental
observations and old quantum theory; and to discuss the necessity of new mechanics and the laws related to
it and their applications. This course also endeavors to make students understand the phenomenon of
thermodynamics and mathematical framework and laws of statistical mechanics, along with their possible
applications.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to-
1. Interpret the basic laws related to quantum mechanics and apply them to solve related problems
2.   Illustrate the concepts of statistical mechanics and solve problems using the same
3. Apply the concepts of statistical physics and thermodynamics to excel in their study of complex
engineering systems
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Introduction to Quantum Physics
Black body radiation, Explanation of it using the photon concept, Photoelectric effect,
Compton effect, de Broglie hypothesis, Experiments demonstrating wave properties of   09
electron: Electron interference (double slit experiment), Electron Diffraction (Davison -
Germer experiment), Uncertainty Principle. Wave-particle duality, Born’s interpretation
of the wave function, Verification of matter waves, Uncertainty principle.
2.   Basic Postulates of Quantum Mechanics
Concept of wave function, Superposition principle of eigenstates. Concept of collapse of
09
wave function. Time dependent and time independent Schrodinger Equation, Concept
of free particle, particle in an infinite and finite potential well.
3.   Concept of Quantum Tunnelling
Reflection and Transmission coefficients. Few realistic examples of tunnelling, e.g., alpha
09
decay, Probe microscopes (Scanning Tunnelling microscope). Simple Harmonic
Oscillator, explanation in 1D (no detailed derivation).
4.   Introduction to Statistical Physics and its Application
Ensembles (Canonical, Micro canonical and Grand canonical) Classical (Maxwell-
Boltzmann) and Quantum statistics, [Bose Einstein (BE) and Fermi Dirac (FD)].   10
Derivation of classical statistics and BE and FD statistics. Equipartition of energy,
Planck’s distribution.

Course Objective
The course would enable students to get a brief introduction of the Indian Constitution and its principles.
The students would have knowledge of concept of ‘State’ and interdependencies of its institutions vis a
vis their relation with fundamental rights.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to-
1. Understand the historic evolution of the Indian Constitution, its drafting, nature and to
understand the principles mentioned in its Preamble
2. Inculcate fundamental rights in its true sense and also the permissible restrictions upon it so as to
enjoy these rights within permissible limits while simultaneously performing their duties and to
apply these principles into their professional lives
3. Ingrain the structure of our polity and role of Judiciary in maintaining the basic structure of the
Constitution
4. Attain knowledge of the Emergency provisions, when and how it is imposed, to know the
additional powers the bestowed upon the Government at times of Emergency and to understand
the Amendment procedure
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Nature, Characteristics and Sources of Indian Constitution   2
2.   Fundamental rights and Fundamental duties – Concept of State, Right to   6

Course Objective

transcoding, understanding and generating time-dependent and space-dependent signals in the
broadest sense. Data is rich and abundant. However, every data wrangler has come across most
of the time this data, which is very noisy in nature. Processing noisy signals and filtering
unwanted part from an image has been a huge concern over the last few decades. Signal and
image processing techniques developed today are very robust and effective models. The objective
is to port some processing techniques from the audio and signal field and use them to process
data. To give basic mathematical understanding of transformation for image and signal

Pre-requisite: Statistical Structures in Data and Inference
Course Objective
The aim of the course is to focus on the basic principles of machine learning and use the concepts for
developing models. The course will emphasize on topics from matrix algebra, calculus, optimization, and
probability theory those are having strong linkage with machine learning
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Recall and define key concepts of machine learning, including types of learning, model evaluation
metrics, and essential terminology. (L1- Remembering)
2. Explain the fundamental differences between supervised vs. unsupervised learning, classification
vs. regression, and concepts like bias-variance. (L2-Understanding)
3. Apply foundational machine learning techniques to both supervised and unsupervised learning
problems, including regression, classification, and dimensionality reduction. (L3- Applying)
4. Assess and interpret model performance using key evaluation metrics, understand the bias-variance
trade-off, and distinguish quality of fit in various settings. (L5 – Evaluating)
5. Understand and apply fundamental concepts of optimization, including gradients, Jacobians,
Hessians, gradient descent, and constrained optimization, with applications to training neural
networks and building feedforward architectures. (L2-Understanding and L3- Applying)
6. Perform and interpret dimensionality reduction techniques, such as Principal Component Analysis
(PCA) and Fisher Discriminant Analysis, and apply support vector machines for classification with
kernel methods and geometric interpretations. ( L4-Analyzing)

Course Objective
The aim of the course is to educate students about the fundamentals of Internet of Things (IoT) and its
building blocks along with their characteristics. It will provide students with understanding of protocols
and standards designed for IoT and the current research on it. It will help students understand the recent
application domains of IoT in everyday life. It will provide information on associated technologies like
cloud computing in the domain of IoT

communication protocols essential for IoT environments. L2 – Understand (Linked to Units 1 & 2)

Pre-requisite: Statistical Structures in Data and Inference
Course Objective
This course provides an introduction to time series analysis. It will educate students on how to choose an
appropriate forecasting method in a particular environment and then apply it using necessary computations.
It aims to equip students with various forecasting techniques and knowledge on modern statistical methods
for analyzing time series data. It will also provide directions to Improve forecasting using better statistical
models based on statistical analysis
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to –
1. Explain the fundamental components of time series data, such as trend, seasonality, and
autocorrelation, and visualize them using various plotting techniques.
2. Apply time series regression models, exponential smoothing, ARMA, ARIMA, and SARIMA
models to forecast univariate and seasonal data.
3. Analyze stationary and non-stationary time series processes using ACF, PACF, unit root tests, and
diagnostics to identify appropriate forecasting models.
4. Evaluate forecasting performance of hierarchical and grouped time series models using
reconciliation methods and compare with alternative approaches.
5. Design advanced forecasting solutions using complex seasonality, the Prophet model, VARs,
bootstrapping, and bagging on real-world datasets using statistical software.

various risk and pricing models that are used in the industry. The purpose of this course is to
give the students exposure to the practical applications of quantitative finance in the real world.
It will teach the students how to put their theoretical understanding into practice
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Describe the structure and characteristics of financial markets and instruments including
equities, bonds, derivatives, and their relevance in time value of money and portfolio
theory.
2. Apply models such as Markowitz Portfolio Theory, CAPM, Fama-French models, and
the Black-Scholes-Merton (BSM) model to evaluate portfolio performance and price
derivatives.
3. Analyze various risk types (market, credit, operational) and model them using
techniques such as Value at Risk (VaR), credit scoring (Z-score), and operational risk
frameworks.
4. Evaluate financial instruments using the no-arbitrage principle, risk-neutral pricing, and
mathematical constructs such as martingales, Markov chains, and Brownian motion in
discrete and continuous time frameworks.
5. Construct and test quantitative finance models by identifying assumptions, verifying
model outputs, and generating counter-examples for incorrect financial statements or
invalid pricing strategies.

Pre-requisite: Knowledge of all core and elective courses completed till 3rd year.
Course Objective
The capstone project is designed to provide a culminating design experience to the final-year students’
learning with essentially required hands-on experience to ensure that they graduate with the required
practical and soft skills. The course aims to encourage students to think critically, solve challenging
problems, do a feasibility study and develop written and oral communication skills, teamwork and
planning. The students may also work in interdisciplinary areas which will help broaden their scope and
learning in different domains.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Select an appropriate problem statement after reviewing the literature and identifying the
research gaps (L1- Remembering)
2. Formulate a feasible design model (L6-Creating)
3. Develop the prototype/proof of concept, test and validate the results (L6- Creating)
4. Create, work in team and apply the solution in practical way to specific problem (L6- Creating)
5. Summarize the major findings to compile a technical report. (L2- Understanding)
Syllabus
A student is required to carry out elaborated project work. The project may be either design and
fabrication work or a simulation and synthesis of a problem/system, and develop algorithms and verify
feasibility of implementation. At the end of the semester students will be required to submit a report
detailing the literature review, design problem formulation, analysis functional simulation and synthesis,
work plan and work done and present his/her work carried out before examiners.

Pre-requisite: Knowledge of all core and elective courses completed till 3rd year.
Course Objective
The capstone project is designed to provide a culminating design experience to the final-year students’
learning with essentially required hands-on experience to ensure that they graduate with the required
practical and soft skills. The course aims to encourage students to think critically, solve challenging
problems, do a feasibility study and develop written and oral communication skills, teamwork and
planning. The students may also work in interdisciplinary areas which will help broaden their scope and
learning in different domains.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Select an appropriate problem statement after reviewing the literature and identifying the research
gaps.
2. Formulate the different use cases/feasible design model.
3. Implement the prototype/proof of concept, test and validate the results.
4. Manage a team project.
5. Summarize the topic into a technical report.
Syllabus
A student is required to carry out elaborated project work. The project may be either design and
fabrication work or a simulation and synthesis of a problem/system, and develop algorithms and
verify feasibility of implementation. At the end of the semester students will be required to submit a
report detailing the literature review, design problem formulation, analysis functional simulation and
synthesis, work plan and work done and present his/her work carried out before examiners.

Pre-requisite: Knowledge of all core and elective courses completed till 3rd year.
Course Objective
The capstone project is designed to provide a culminating design experience to the final-year students’
learning with essentially required hands-on experience to ensure that they graduate with the required
practical and soft skills. The course aims to encourage students to think critically, solve challenging
problems, do a feasibility study and develop written and oral communication skills, teamwork and
planning. The students may also work in interdisciplinary areas which will help broaden their scope and
learning in different domains.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Select an appropriate problem statement after reviewing the literature and identifying the research
gaps.
2. Formulate the different use cases/feasible design model.
3. Implement the prototype/proof of concept, test and validate the results.
4. Manage a team project.
5. Summarize the topic into a technical report.
Syllabus
A student is required to carry out elaborated project work. The project may be either design and
fabrication work or a simulation and synthesis of a problem/system, and develop algorithms and
verify feasibility of implementation. At the end of the semester students will be required to submit a
report detailing the literature review, design problem formulation, analysis functional simulation and
synthesis, work plan and work done and present his/her work carried out before examiners.

Course Objective

This course is aimed to teach the drawbacks of classical physics in explaining several experimental
observations and old quantum theory; and to discuss the necessity of new mechanics and the laws related to
it and their applications. This course also endeavors to make students understand the phenomenon of
thermodynamics and mathematical framework and laws of statistical mechanics, along with their possible
applications.

Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to-
1. Explain the basic laws related to quantum mechanics and apply them to solve related problems
2. Elucidate the concepts of statistical mechanics and solve problems using the same
3. Apply the concepts of statistical physics and thermodynamics to excel in their study of complex
engineering systems

electron: Electron interference (double slit experiment), Electron Diffraction (Davison -
Germer experiment), Uncertainty Principle. Wave-particle duality, Born’s interpretation
of the wave function, Verification of matter waves, Uncertainty principle.

wave function. Time dependent and time independent Schrodinger Equation, Concept
of free particle, particle in an infinite and finite potential well.

fundamental vector calculus theorems such as Green’s, Stokes’, and Gauss’ theorems to
evaluate integrals. (K3)

world problems in physics, engineering, and applied sciences. (K3)

5. Explain the principles of metabolism and energy transactions, and categorize microorganisms
based on their characteristics, growth kinetics, and applications in biotechnology and drug
discovery. (K1)

Pre-requisite: Introduction to IT Systems.
Course Objective
This course is designed to take students through IT infrastructure landscape as an overview of
different building blocks and their functionalities. It will give students an idea about the different
roles as IT engineers can play in IT infrastructure domain.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, student would be able to-
1. Describe IT infrastructure Architecture building blocks and their relevant concepts
2. Study the overview of Database, Network, Storage Systems, cloud-based systems
3. Explain various Roles and responsibilities in IT landscape as IT engineer
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1   IT Infrastructure Building Blocks and Concepts   3
Definition of IT infrastructure, IT building blocks: Processes / Information
building block, Applications building block, Infrastructure building blocks.
2   IT Infrastructure Performance Concepts   2
Performance of infrastructure design vs Performance of a running system.
Performance testing, Scalability, Load balancing, Capacity management.
3   Network overview   5
Types of networks, Layers concepts, Different Protocols, Network Topologies,
Switching concepts, IP addressing, Routing, Virtual LAN
Security overview: Firewall, Security basics, Security components, Encryption-
decryption, key encryptions, data security, network security.
Data Centers – Physical Infrastructure and Storage
4   Database overview   5
Database System Applications, Purpose of Database Systems, View of Data,
Database Languages, Data Models, Database Users, Files base vs DBMS
SQL vs NoSQL, Introduction Data mining and data warehouse.
5   Storage overview   5
Storage Overview, What is Storage Networking Technology?, Types of Storage
Systems, Storage Devices and Technologies, RAID Functions, RAID Types,
Archiving Data and data policy, Data storage Techniques, Optical Storage, Solid
State Drives, Introduction to Storage Area Networks, Cloud-based storage
services.

This course introduces approaches used to solve problems using computing, which are not based
on traditional hardcoded programs. These solutions are based on mathematical modeling of
problem. It helps students to gain insight in developing more flexible applications and effective
solutions especially in context of complex problems.

After completion of the course, students would be able to-
1. Explain various problem solving methods and tools using soft computing.
2. Describe Fuzzy logic, Genetic Algorithm concepts and its applications.
3. Explain working of different Machine learning techniques, Artificial Neural Networks (ANN)
and their applications.

Course Objective

opportunity to students to explore various societal problems and provide innovative solutions for
the same. The course encourage students to develop technical and soft skills. The students may
also work in interdisciplinary areas which will help broaden their scope and learning in different
domains.
Course Outcomes

2. Implement the prototype/proof of concept using fundamental and disciplinary concepts and
methods.
3. Manage a team project.

Syllabus
A student group is required to identify some real world problem and develop a solution using
design and critical thinking principles. They may develop a working model or a proof of concept
of the solution. At the end of the semester, students will submit a report detailing the problem
analysis process and designed solution. Each group will present their work before examiners.

Pre-requisite: Knowledge of fundamental concepts in Algebra, Differential
and Integral Calculus.
Course Objective
This course aims to instil in prospective engineer’s knowledge of concepts and techniques
in Linear Algebra and Differential Equations. It also prepares the students to deal with
advanced level of Mathematics and applications that would be essential for their disciplines.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to-
1. Understand the fundamental concepts of linear algebra, including vector spaces, subspaces,
basis, and dimension, and apply them to solve problems related to linear independence and
dependence.
2. Analyze and apply linear transformations, eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and diagonalization
techniques, including the Rank-Nullity Theorem and the Cayley-Hamilton Theorem, to
solve problems involving matrices.
3. Solve first-order ordinary differential equations using exact equations, integrating factors,
and special methods such as Bernoulli’s equation and orthogonal trajectories.
4. Formulate and solve higher-order linear differential equations using methods such as the
operator method, undetermined coefficients, variation of parameters, and power series
solutions, including Legendre and Bessel equations.
5. Understand the formation and classification of partial differential equations and apply direct
integration and separation of variables techniques to solve them in Cartesian coordinates.
6. Apply concepts from linear algebra and differential equations to model and solve real-world
problems in engineering, physics, and applied sciences.

Course Objective
The course provide basic orientation towards microeconomic principles and help them understand the
functions of management. This course also aims to understand issues dealing with small-scale economic
phenomena and concepts such as prices and output of firms, industries and resource owners along with
examining market impact of technological change with regards to understand broader aspects of the
economy and its environment.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Understand Fundamental Economic Concepts - Explain the basic concepts of economics,
including scarcity of resources, economic systems, and demand-supply analysis. (K1, K2)
2. Demonstrate Consumer and Producer Behavior - Apply utility analysis and production
theories to understand consumer decision-making and cost structures in different market
conditions (K2, K3)
3. Illustrate Market Structures and Pricing Mechanisms - Differentiate between market
structures such as monopoly, oligopoly, perfect and imperfect competition, and explain
price and output determination. (K2, K3)
4. Apply Management Principles in Decision-Making - Demonstrate an understanding of
management functions such as planning, organizing, decision-making, and leadership
based on classical and modern theories. (K2, K3)
5. Understand the Role of Business Functions in Organizational Success - Examine the
significance of key business functions such as finance, marketing, human resources, and
operations, and their interdependence in achieving organizational objectives. (K1, K2)

Course Objective
The principal objective of the course is to train the students in the construction and
understanding of mathematical proofs and common mathematical arguments. It will instil
sound knowledge of different topics of discrete mathematics which students will readily
apply in the subsequent courses of their programme.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Understand fundamental concepts of discrete mathematics, including set theory,
relations, functions, logic, and proof techniques. (K2)
2. Apply mathematical logic, predicate calculus, and proof techniques, including
mathematical induction, to establish the validity of statements and theorems. (K3)
3. Analyse problems involving combinatorics, recurrence relations, generating
functions, and the pigeonhole principle to model discrete structures. (K4)
4. Interpret graphs and trees, including their properties, colouring, connectivity, and
spanning trees, and apply algorithms like Kruskal’s and Prim’s to solve network-
related problems. (K3, K4)
5. Formulate concepts from abstract algebra, including groups, rings, and fields, to
construct mathematical models and solve real-world problems. (K5)

Pre-requisite: Knowledge of Basic concepts in Number theory and Algebra.
Objectives-
The principal objective of the course is to train the students in the construction and
understanding of mathematical proofs and common mathematical arguments. It will instil
sound knowledge of different topics of discrete mathematics which students will readily
apply in the subsequent courses of their programme.
Course Outcomes-
After completion of the course, students will be able to-
1. Understand fundamental concepts of discrete mathematics, including set theory,
relations, functions, logic, and proof techniques. (K2)
2. Apply mathematical logic, predicate calculus, and proof techniques, including
mathematical induction, to establish the validity of statements and theorems. (K3)
3. Analyse problems involving combinatorics, recurrence relations, generating functions,
and the pigeonhole principle to model discrete structures. (K4)
4. Interpret graphs and trees, including their properties, colouring, connectivity, and
spanning trees, and apply algorithms like Kruskal’s and Prim’s to solve network-related
problems. (K3, K4)
5. Formulate concepts from abstract algebra, including groups, rings, and fields, to construct
mathematical models and solve real-world problems. (K5)

Course Objective
This course helps to develop and analyse continuous and discrete time signals and systems. It also forms the
foundation for further studies in the areas such as speech/audio processing, image processing, and
communication systems.
Course outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Illustrate the fundamental concepts of signals and systems, including classification and operations
on signals. (L2 - Understanding)
2. Explain the properties of Linear Time-Invariant (LTI) systems and apply convolution techniques.
(L2 - Understanding)
3. Illustrate the Fourier series representation of periodic signals, analyze their magnitude, and phase
spectra. (L2 - Understanding)

This course introduces the fundamental concepts and techniques underlying the construction of
digital systems. It further provides insight into designing digital logic circuits using basic building
blocks and necessary techniques required in computer hardware design.
Course Outcomes

codes. (L2 - Understanding)

(L4 - Analyzing)
3. Build combinational logic circuits such as adders, multiplexers, decoders, and encoders. (L3

4. Analyze sequential circuits, including flip-flops, registers, and counters. (L4 - Analyzing)

the fundamental concepts of different materials and its stresses, application of fluids, functioning
of thermal and energy systems. Students also understands the concepts of different motions and
power transmission in the mechanical engineering domain.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Describe the role of mechanical engineering in the industry and society
2. Design things that work, that are cost effective to manufacture, safe to use, and are
responsible in terms of their environmental impact
3. Acquire the basic knowledge of various elements of mechanical engineering

Course Objective
The course is aimed at imparting knowledge of the deformable bodies subjected to different types of

loading. This course will help students to determine the failure criteria of a body subjected to various
stresses. Students will be able to identify the different tests to be performed on the materials.

fundamental vector calculus theorems such as Green’s, Stokes’, and Gauss’ theorems to
evaluate integrals. (K3)

world problems in physics, engineering, and applied sciences. (K3)

Pre-requisite: Knowledge of fundamental concepts in Algebra, Differential

Course Objective
This course aims to instil in prospective engineer’s knowledge of concepts and techniques
in Linear Algebra and Differential Equations. It also prepares the students to deal with
advanced level of Mathematics and applications that would be essential for their disciplines.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to-
1. Understand the fundamental concepts of linear algebra, including vector spaces, subspaces,
basis, and dimension, and apply them to solve problems related to linear independence and
dependence.
2. Analyze and apply linear transformations, eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and diagonalization
techniques, including the Rank-Nullity Theorem and the Cayley-Hamilton Theorem, to
solve problems involving matrices.
3. Solve first-order ordinary differential equations using exact equations, integrating factors,
and special methods such as Bernoulli’s equation and orthogonal trajectories.
4. Formulate and solve higher-order linear differential equations using methods such as the
operator method, undetermined coefficients, variation of parameters, and power series
solutions, including Legendre and Bessel equations.
5. Understand the formation and classification of partial differential equations and apply direct
integration and separation of variables techniques to solve them in Cartesian coordinates.
6. Apply concepts from linear algebra and differential equations to model and solve real-world
problems in engineering, physics, and applied sciences.

Pre-requisite: Fundamental knowledge of physics, chemistry, and mathematics.
Course Objective:

disciplinary field, to make them aware of the application of engineering principles in biology. This
will encourage engineering students to think about solving biological problems with engineering
tools. They will also be exposed to the application of engineering principles in biology and
engineering robust solutions inspired by biological examples.

transcription, and translation, and interpret Mendel's laws and their significance in genetics. (K2)

inhibition, and discuss their industrial and biological applications. (K2)

discovery. (K1)

Pre-requisite: Nil
Course Objective
In this course students will get acquainted with the various systems of forces. It is designed for the
students to understand the concept of static equilibrium and apply the equations of motion to rigid
bodies.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Identify and solve force systems using fundamental principles of mechanics to understand
their effects on engineering structures and components
2. Apply equilibrium conditions to determine support reactions, internal forces, and assess the
stability of various structures
3. Identify centroids and moments of inertia of engineering components, utilizing the parallel
and perpendicular axis theorems for structural analysis
4. Analyze particle motion using velocity, acceleration, and different coordinate systems
5. Apply Newton’s laws, D'Alembert's principle under translational motion, rotational motion
to solve particle motion problems
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1. System of Forces   05
Rectangular components of forces in space, moment, couple, Varignon’s theorem,
resolution of forces, resultant of force system (coplanar, non-coplanar), concept
of virtual work, principle of virtual work.
2. Application of System of Forces and Equilibrium   08
Conditions of equilibrium, types of support, loads and beams, free body
diagrams, support reactions.
Friction
Laws of friction, angle of friction, angle of repose, cone of friction, equilibrium of
bodies on rough horizontal and inclined plane, application to inclined planes,
wedges, ladder & screw jack.
Analysis of Pin Jointed Plane Trusses
Perfect truss, analysis using method of joints and method of sections.
3. Centroid and Moment of Inertia   03
Centroid, moment of inertia, polar moment of inertia, and product of inertia,
parallel and perpendicular axis theorem.
4. Kinematics of Particle   07
Velocity and acceleration in terms of rectangular coordinate system, rectilinear
motion, curvilinear motion, projectile motion, tangential and normal component
of acceleration, acceleration - time, velocity- time graphs and their uses, relative
velocity
B Tech-Integrated /Mechanical/Sem-VII/2026-27/Page 1
SVKM’s NMIMS Deemed-to-be University
Mukesh Patel School of Technology Management and Engineering
Kinematics of Rigid Bodies
Translation, pure rotation and plane motion of rigid bodies, instantaneous centre
of rotation for the velocity for bodies in plane motion, link mechanisms (up to
two links).
5. Kinetics of Particles   07
Newton’s laws of motion, D’Alembert’s principle, equation of dynamic
equilibrium, linear motion, curvilinear motion.
Kinetics of Rigid Bodies
D’Alembert’s principle for bodies under translational motion, rotational motion
about a fixed axis and plane motion.
Total   30

Pre-requisite: Physics, Chemistry
Course Objective
The course is aimed at imparting basic knowledge of science of materials and physical
metallurgy. This course introduces and cements the concept of structure property correlations.
It is designed to lay the foundation for the detailed understanding of mechanical behavior of
materials, phase diagrams, heat treatment and failure of materials. The students are also
introduced to certain applications of ferrous, non-ferrous and new age materials.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Relate mechanical properties with the mechanical processing of materials
2. Demonstrate the mechanical behaviour of metals using destructive and non-destructive
testing
3. Analyze the root cause of failure in different types of materials
4. Interpret Phase Transformations in Iron-Iron Carbon Alloys
5. Recommend suitable heat treatment processes with the help of phase diagrams.
Detailed Syllabus
Unit Description   Duration
1   Mechanical Behavior of Metals   05
Deformation
Crystal structures and imperfections, elastic and plastic deformation.
Deformation in single crystal and polycrystalline materials. Cold and Hot
working of materials and Strain hardening of metals. Recrystallization
annealing, recovery and grain growth.
2   Testing of Materials   04
Destructive Testing
Basic mechanical properties, tensile testing, hardness testing, Impact testing.
Non-Destructive Testing
Dye Penetrant, Magnetic Particle and Ultrasonic testing.
3   Failure of Metals   05
Fracture: Definition and types of fracture.
Fatigue: Definition and significance of cyclic stress, mechanism of fatigue
failure. S-N curve and its interpretation, Notch effect, surface effect,
Corrosion and thermal fatigue.
Creep: Definition and significance of creep, analysis of classical creep curve,
creep resistant materials.

Mukesh Patel School of Technology Management and Engineering
4   Phase Diagrams   05
Concept of solidification of metals, Solidification of pure metals, solid
solutions. Hume Rothery rules, Phase rule, Cooling curves, Important binary
phase diagrams, isomorphous system, Eutectic system, Eutectoid system,
Peritectic system, Gibb’s phase rule, Lever rule.
5   Fe-Fe3C Equilibrium Diagram
Importance of iron as engineering material, Allotropic forms of irons.   05
Fe-Fe3C Diagram
Phases, reactions, microstructures and critical temperatures.
Effect of Alloying Elements in Steels   02
Engineering Alloys, Significance of alloying elements.
6   Heat Treatment of Steel   04
Definition and significance of heat treatment, Time temperature
transformation diagrams (TTT), Continuous cooling Transformation (CCT).
Heat treatment processes: Annealing, Normalizing, Hardening and
Tempering.
