2   2   0   3   Marks Scaled to 50   Marks Scaled to 50
Pre-requisite: Engineering Mechanics, Fluid Mechanics and Strength of Materials
Course Objective
This course introduces the basic concepts of vibrations and discusses free vibration of an undamped
single-degree of-freedom system. This course also deals with two-degree-of-freedom systems, which
require two independent coordinates to describe their motion. The modeling of continuous
systems as multidegree-of-freedom systems is also presented in this course.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Derive the equation of motion of a single-degree-of-freedom system
2. Solve two-degree-of-freedom free- and forced-vibration problems
3. Formulate the equations of motion of multidegree-of-freedom systems
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Fundamentals of Vibration   07
Basic Concepts of Vibration, Classification of Vibration, Vibration Analysis
Procedure, Spring Elements, Mass or Inertia Elements, Damping Elements,
Harmonic Motion, Harmonic Analysis
2.   Single-Degree-of-Freedom Systems   08
Free Vibration of an Undamped Translational System, Free Vibration of an
Undamped Torsional System, Free Vibration with Viscous Damping, Free
Vibration with Coulomb Damping.
3.   Two-Degree-of-Freedom Systems   06
Equations of Motion for Forced Vibration, Free Vibration Analysis of an
Undamped System, Torsional System, Forced-Vibration Analysis.
4.   Multidegree-of-Freedom Systems   09
Modeling of Continuous Systems as Multi degree of Freedom Systems, Equations
of Motion, Influence Coefficients, Generalized Coordinates and Generalized
Forces, Lagrange s Equations, Equations of Motion of Undamped Systems in
Matrix Form, Eigenvalue Problem
Total   30
Text Books
1. S. S. Rao, Mechanical Vibration, Addison Wesley, 2004.
2. Michel Géradin and Daniel J. Rixen, Mechanical Vibrations Theory and Application to Structural
Dynamics, John Wiley & Sons, 2015.

Course Objective
The objective of the course is to familiarize with basic knowledge of Additive Manufacturing (AM)
and its capabilities in the modern digital manufacturing industries. It teaches about various
additive manufacturing techniques.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Compare the fundamental principles of various additive manufacturing technologies in terms
of material requirements, manufacturing technologies and applications
2. Identify critical areas where AM can be applied to create value for the product
3. Apply the necessary skills in selecting the right AM process for a given application

Introduction to AM, history of AM, definition, distinction between AM, CNC
& other digital manufacturing techniques, reasons to use AM, classifications
of AM processes, design for additive manufacturing (DfAM), AM industry:
present and future, AM process chain, AM file formats (STL, 3MF, AMF, PLY,

Objective
The objective of this course is to help the students understand the principles and applications
relevant to the planning, design, and operations of manufacturing or service firms. This course
also develops an understanding about quality management practices in organizations that
facilitate organizational effectiveness.
Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Develop an understanding of manufacturing and service operations management as a
subject and outline the strategic concerns involved in operations decisions
2. Apply the principles, philosophy underpinning inventory management techniques, just-
in-time and MRP systems along with their limitations
3. Analyze the economic aspects related to production management

Meaning of production, production process system, scope of production
management, objectives of production management, functions and scopes
of production management, scope of production management, brief history
of production management, responsibilities of production manager.
2.   Productivity   04

productivity improvement, measurement of productivity.

scheduling, line balancing.

Course Objective
This course focusses on a critical understanding and strategic importance of operations management.
The students can get familiar with interactions between firms based on parameters such as
information sharing, contracting and coordination in supply chain management.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Evaluate the application of operations management policies and techniques to the service
sector as well as manufacturing firms
2. Analyze and organize Global Network Logistics for trade and transport systems, sourcing and
procurement
3. Apply the latest developments in information technology to supply chain management in
order to generate greater benefit

Introduction, meaning, nature and scope of production and operations
management. Difference between production and operations management.
Productivity, factors affecting productivity and productivity measurement. Work
study— Method study and work measurement. Production Technology – Types
of manufacturing processes. Plant location and types of plant layout.
2.   Material and Inventory Management   10
Types of production planning, process of production planning and control (PPC)
– routing, scheduling and loading. Master production schedule, aggregate
production planning. Types of inventories, inventory control techniques- EOQ,
ABC, VED, FSN, HML and SDE (Simple numerical problems on Inventory control
techniques).

facilities, information obstacles to achieving fit.

Pre-requisite: Mathematics I, Mathematics II, Engineering Mechanics, Strength of Materials, Heat
Transfer
Course Objective
This course presents an introduction to the finite element methods. The guidelines for selecting
displacement functions and the concepts that should be considered when modeling are discussed as
the course progresses. This course describes how to treat different types of forces for two-dimensional
elements and to solve one-dimensional heat transfer problems.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to –
1. Understanding the basic principles of FEA, including discretization, element types and shape
functions
2. Derive the stiffness matrix for the beam and Constant-Strain Triangular element
3. Illustrate FEA characteristic equations to analyze plain stress, plain strain and derive element
matrices for CST elements
4. Develop FEA Characteristic equations for Isoparamteric problems and heat transfer problem
5. Analyze solution accuracy by performing error estimation, mesh refinement studies, and
convergence analysis to improve simulation reliability
6. Use ANSYS in real-world mechanical, thermal, and structural engineering problems to analyze
their behavior
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Introduction   07
Brief history, matrix notation, general steps, applications and advantages of the
FEM, computer programs for the FEM, stiffness matrix for a spring element,
spring assemblage, direct stiffness method, boundary conditions.
2.   Truss   08
Stiffness matrix for a bar element, displacement function, transformation of
vectors in two dimensions, global stiffness matrix for bar arbitrarily oriented in
the plane, computation of stress for a bar in the x – y plane, solution of a plane
truss, use of symmetry in structures, inclined supports.
3.   Beam and Frame   10
Beam stiffness, assemblage of beam stiffness matrices, direct stiffness method,
distributed loading, beam element with nodal hinge, two-dimensional arbitrarily
oriented beam element, rigid plane frame, skewed supports, beam element
arbitrarily oriented in space, concept of substructure analysis

Mukesh Patel School of Technology Management and Engineering
4.   Plane Stress and Plane Strain   07
Concepts of Plane Stress and Plane Strain, Constant-Strain Triangular Element
Stiffness Matrix, Body and Surface Forces, Plane Stress Problem, Bilinear
Rectangle, Comparison of Elements
5.   Practical Considerations in Modeling   05
Finite Element Modeling, Equilibrium and Compatibility of Finite Element
Results, Convergence of Solution and Mesh Refinement.
6.   Heat Transfer and Mass Transport   08
Basic Differential Equation, Heat Transfer with Convection, Thermal
Conductivities, Heat Transfer Coefficients, One-Dimensional and Two-
Dimensional Finite Element Formulation, Line or Point Sources,   One-
Dimensional Heat Transfer with Mass Transport
Total   45

Pre-requisite: Engineering Physics
Course Objective
The objective of this course is to develop awareness and basic skills necessary for the reliable
measurements and measuring instruments and impart knowledge on methods of measurement of
different engineering parameters such as pressure, temperature, displacement, etc. and different
metrological instruments for linear, angular, taper and surface finish measurements.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to –
1. Describe various terminologies associated with measurement and metrology
2. Understand the objectives of metrology, methods of measurement, standards of measurement
& various measurement parameters
3. Choose sensors, devices and methods for measurement of specific parameters with required
accuracy
4. Demonstrate the ability to apply precision measurement techniques to ensure accuracy and
quality control in mechanical systems
5. Measure and derive important dimensions of thread forms and gears
6. Analyze the impact of various factors on the measurement process
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Introduction to Measurement   04
Need of measurement, Study of instruments, measurement methods, generalized
measurement system & its functional elements, instrument characteristics - static
& dynamic characteristics, calibration.
2.   Temperature and Pressure Measurement   10
Thermometry
Overview   of thermometry, thermometers,   thermo-electric temperature
measurement, resistance thermometry, pyrometer.
Pressure Measurement
Bourdon tubes, dead weight pressure gauge tester, diaphragm gauge, LVDT,
Piezo-electric pressure gauge, Low vacuum gauges - McLeod gauge, thermal
conductivity gauge, Pirani gauge, ionization gauge, comparison of different
pressure measuring instruments.

(analytical treatment), analysis of Wheatstone’s network using strain gauges,
mounting of strain gauges.
4.   Measurement Standards, Comparators and Angular Measurement   10
Definition and concept of metrology, measurement standards, types and sources
of errors, accuracy and precision, introduction to uncertainty in measurement,
Calibration
Concept and procedure.
Length Standards
Line and end standards, slip gauges and linear measuring instruments.
Angular Measurement
Angle standards, sine bar, angle gauges, autocollimator, angle dekkor, optical
square, taper measurement, universal bevel protractor.
Interferometry
Basic principles, source of light, optical flats, fringe pattern and their
interpretation.
5.   Comparators, Thread and Gear Metrology, Surface Roughness Measurement   10
Comparators
Types, construction and working of Mechanical, Optical, Electrical, Pneumatic
comparators.
Screw Thread Metrology
Screw thread terminology, measurement of thread parameters, study of thread
gauges, floating carriage micrometer.
Gear Metrology
Gear profile and measurement of parameters, study of tool maker’s microscope
and profile projector.
Surface Roughness Measurement
Surface texture, assessment of surface roughness, Tomlinson surface meter, and
other surface measuring devices.
6.   Advances in Metrology   07
Coordinate measuring machine (CMM)
Fundamental features of CMM, role of CMMs, types of CMM and applications,
types of probe.
Laser Metrology
Basic concepts of lasers, advantages of lasers, laser interferometers, types,
applications.

Vision system measurement, multisensory systems.

Introduction to nano metrology.

Course Objective

learning with essentially required hands-on experience to ensure that they graduate with the required
practical and soft skills. The course aims to encourage students to think critically, solve challenging
problems, do a feasibility study and develop written and oral communication skills, teamwork and
planning. The students may also work in interdisciplinary areas which will help broaden their scope and
learning in different domains.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Select an appropriate problem statement after reviewing the literature and identifying the research
gaps

A student is required to carry out elaborated project work. The project may be either design and
fabrication work or a simulation and synthesis of a problem/system, and develop algorithms and
verify feasibility of implementation. At the end of the semester students will be required to submit a
report detailing the literature review, design problem formulation, analysis functional simulation and
synthesis, work plan and work done and present his/her work carried out before examiners.

Pre-requisite: Basic Electrical Engineering, Engineering Mechanics and Strength of Materials
Course Objective
This course presents an introduction to wind energy and wind turbines. It introduces the current
challenges in modern wind turbine analysis, design, and development and provides a comprehensive
examination of state-of-the-art technologies.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to –
1. Categorize various types of wind turbines and its principal components
2. Determine the mechanical power, types of stresses and the control parameters
3. Analyze the economics, effects on the environment, safety in operation and the potential hazards
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Introduction   10
Importance of renewable, technical issues, wind farm development, wind turbine
siting, new and future technologies, energy in a moving object and moving fluid,
power in the wind, power absorption by a turbine, wind speed variation, force
from wind, aerodynamic force, lift and drag coefficients, airfoils.
2.   Types and Components of Wind Turbine   10
Turbine classification, propeller wind turbine, The H-rotor, Darrieus turbine,
Savonius rotor, mechanical components - tower, foundation, rotor, nacelle,
gearbox, turbine brake, electrical components - generators, transformers and
anemometer.
3.   Propeller   05
Mechanical power, diagrams, mechanical power in a turbine, turbine power
variation with angular speed, daily energy production by a turbine, annual energy
production.
4.   Wind Turbine Design   10
Power accord with the wind speed, wind speed measurement, power calculations,
output power quality and requirement, blade pitch control, turbine operating
power curve, yaw control, parking brake, fault control, various operational states
of a turbine, loads on the rotor, aerodynamic loads on the blade, other blade loads,
vibrations, blade fatigue, blade construction.

comparison with other energy sources, cost per unit, onshore wind farms, noise,
view, landscape, effects on birds, RF interference and effect on communications,
offshore wind farms, effects on birds and marine animals, safety and working
with wind turbines, effect of temperature and environmental changes, protection
from lightning, ice forming on the blades, wind energy in urban areas, working

improve product quality and process efficiency by identifying and measuring production process
variability, which, if not successfully addressed can lead to inconsistent product quality, costly
wastage, and other reliability and productivity problems.

aimed at giving in-depth idea of the different techniques used in micro and nano

Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to:

Detailed Syllabus: (per session plan )
Unit   Description   Duration
1   Basic Concepts   15
Modes of Heat Transfer, its mechanism and mathematical models.
Conduction Heat Transfer:
Fourier’s general conduction equation in Cartesian, Cylindrical
and Spherical co-ordinates (no derivations in cylindrical and
spherical coordinates), thermal resistance, solution of Fourier’s
equation for one dimensional steady state heat conduction
through various configurations such as plane, cylindrical,
spherical wall, composite medium. Critical thickness of insulation
and its importance.
Heat Transfer from extended surfaces:
Types of fins, Governing equation, fin effectiveness, efficiency of
fins, concept of corrected fin length, application of fins.
Unsteady State Heat Conduction: Lumped System Analysis
2   Convection Heat Transfer:   15
Forced and natural convection, hydrodynamic and thermal
boundary layer, Convection heat transfer coefficient, Momentum
and energy equation for laminar boundary layer, Laminar and
Turbulent flow, principles of dimensional analysis, physical
significance of dimensionless numbers, Nusselt number, Prandtl
number, Reynolds number, Grashof number.

body and radiation properties. Microwave Heating.
Basic laws of radiation;   Planck’s law, Kirchoff’s law, Stefan-
Boltzman law, Wein’s-displacement law and Lambert’s Cosine
law, Intensity of radiation, radiosity, shape factor for simple
geometries, heat exchange between non-black bodies, Radiation
Shield.

flow arrangement, overall heat transfer coefficient, fouling factor,

method.

Course Objective
This course provides the general steps used in the finite element methods and analysis of one and
two-dimensional problems. It also discusses different field problems, which relate to structural, fluid
and thermal engineering domains.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Describe the basic procedures and applications of FEA
2. Apply FEA to heat transfer and fluid flow problems in the field
3. Analyze the stiffness matrix for a bar, beam and plane elements

penalty method, stress-strain and reaction calculations

quadrilateral.

Pre-requisite: Manufacturing Processes – I & II , Materials Engineering
Course Objective
This course provides comprehensive understanding and analysis of conventional metal forming
processes such as forging, rolling, extrusion, sheet metal working and also includes recently developed
forming processes.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Connect the forming processes with their defects and remedies to avoid defective products
2. Analyse the different metal forming operations like forging, rolling, blanking, coining and
extrusion
3. Summarize the advanced metal forming processes used in the industries
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Fundamentals of Metal Forming   09
Introduction of forming processes. Concept of Formability, formability limits and
formability diagram. Wire and Tube Drawing- Introduction rod and wire drawing
machines - construction and working. Preparation of stock for wire drawing. Wire
drawing dies, material and design. Heat treatment, variables in wire drawing,
Maximum reduction in wire in one pass, forces required in drawing. Multiple
drawing, defects in drawing and remedies, work hardening, lubrication in wire
drawing. Tube drawing: Methods, force calculations. Lubrication in tube drawing.
2.   Forging   07
Introduction, classification of forging processes, forging equipment- Hammers,
presses, furnaces etc. construction working capacities and selection of equipment.
Basic forging operations such as drawing, fullering edging, blocking etc.
Forgeability tests, design of forging as a product, friction in forging. Forging defects
and the remedies. New technologies: liquid metal forging, isothermal forging, draft
forging, Rotary swaging, Roll forging, lubrication in forging.
3.   Rolling of Metals   08
Scope and importance of rolling. Effect of grain direction in rolling Types of Rolling
Mills- construction and working. Deformation in rolling and determination forces
required. Process variables, redundant deformation, Roll bite and friction. Roll
flattening, Roll camber - its effect on rolling process, mill spring. Defects in rolling.
Automatic gauge control- Roll pass classification & design. Lubrication in rolling.

Mukesh Patel School of Technology Management and Engineering
4.   Sheet Metal Working   07
Sheet Metal properties, gauges and surface conditions. Various cutting and forming
operations, types of dies used, force requirement, theory of shear, methods of force
reduction, defects, lubricants used. Miscellaneous sheet metal working operations:
Metal spinning, fine blanking, coining, embossing, rubber forming, stretch forming.
Coining Embossing, Curling, Spinning and fine blanking.
5.   Extrusion   07
Extrusion types: Direct, reverse, impact, hydrostatic extrusion. Dies for extrusion,
stock penetration. Extrusion ratio of force equipment (with and without friction),
metal flow in extrusion, defects. Role of friction and lubricants. Manufacture of
seam-less tubes.
6.   Advanced Metal Forming Processes   07
Introduction to High velocity forming- principles, comparison of high velocity and
conventional forming processes. Explosive forming, Magnetic pulse forming,
electro hydraulic forming. Stretch forming, flow forming advantages, limitations
and application of the process.
Total   45

concepts of theoretical and experimental techniques in stress-analysis. It also aims to impart a
comprehensive understanding of the stress and strain measurements with mathematical and
experimental perspectives.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Apply the theoretical concepts of stress and strain in measurement procedures
2.   Articulate principal stress measurement by the photoelastic technique on 2-Dimensional and
3-Dimensional objects
3. Apply strain gauges for strain measurement with understanding of different mounting
approaches

This course provides in-depth details about steam, hydro, nuclear, gas turbine power plants which
play an important role in power generation along with recent advances and plant economics.
Course Outcomes

1. Discuss the working principle and basic components of the various types of power plants.
2. Analyze the working and layout of power plants and the different systems comprising the
plant and discuss about its economic and safety impacts.

selection of the plants, review of basic thermodynamic cycles used in power plants.

various curves for estimating stream flow and size of reservoir, power plants

Pre-requisite: Manufacturing Processes I and II, Machine Drawing, CAD/CAM/CIM
Course Objective
The objective of the course is to introduce students to Additive Manufacturing (AM) and its
capabilities in the modern digital manufacturing industry. It is structured to familiarize students
with operating principles and applications of most prominent technologies in the field of Additive
Manufacturing.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Relate the fundamental principles of various Additive Manufacturing (AM) technologies,
material requirements and cost considerations with regards to each AM process
2. Identify critical areas where AM can be applied to create value for the entire product life-cycle
3. Apply the necessary skills in selecting the right AM process for a given application
Detailed Syllabus
Unit Description   Duration
1.   Introduction to Additive Manufacturing   04
Introduction to AM, history of AM, definition, distinction between AM, CNC &
other digital manufacturing techniques, reasons to use AM, classifications of AM
processes, design for Additive Manufacturing (DfAM), AM industry: present and
future, AM process chain, CAD and file formats for AM.
2.   Extrusion based AM processes   05
Fused deposition Modelling (FDM), history of FDM, material requirements,
workflow: material loading, liquefaction, bonding, solidification, support
generation, nozzle dynamics, applications, benefits and limitations,   post-
processing, material characterization, extrusion of: ceramics, metals, biomaterials,
composites, non-planer systems, contour crafting, concrete printing.
3.   Vat Polymerization AM process   05
Stereolithography apparatus (SLA), history of SLA, material requirements,
workflow: SLA chemistry, reaction mechanism, scan patterns, applications,
benefits and limitations, other liquid polymer-based systems: solid ground curing
SGC, Microstreolithography, Digital Light Processing DLP, Continuous Liquid
Interface Production CLIP, Large-Scale Rapid Liquid Printing.
4.   Sheet Lamination AM Processes   04
Laminated Object Manufacturing (LOM), LOM of paper, polymer and composite
sheets, LOM mechanism: gluing, adhesive bonding, bond then from, from then
bond, thermal bonding,   sheet metal clamping, Ultrasonic Additive
Manufacturing(UAM), ultrasonic welding fundamentals, UAM process
parameters, material characterization.

powder production methods, powder fusion mechanism, polymer ageing and
recycling, High Speed Sintering(HSS), Multi-Jet Fusion(MJF), polymer powder
characterization and selection, Selective Laser Melting (SLM): process workflow
and material requirements, powder melting mechanism, melt pool dynamics,
laser scan patterns, post-processing, powder production, handling and recycling,
Electron Beam Melting (EBM) Process.
6.   Binder Jetting (BJ) & Material Jetting AM Process   06
Workflow, thermal and piezoelectric inkjet, material requirements, material
jetting fluid mechanics, drop-on-demand and continuous methods of MJ, material
jetting of metals, ceramics, nanomaterial, BJ AM Process: process workflow,
material requirements, powder characterization for BJ process, binder-powder

Process workflow, materials feeding for DED: powder (Laser Engineered Net
Shaping) & wire, process parameters and optimization, Electron Beam Additive
Manufacturing (EBAM) plasma-based DED, Cold Spray.

Course Objective
This course focusses on the application of classical mechanics to various biological problems by
combining the fields of biology and physiology. This course is concerned with the application of
principles of mechanics to the conceptualization, design, development and analysis of equipment
and systems as applied to human body.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Correlate mechanics, biomechanics and kinesiology and differentiate between their uses in the
analysis of human movement
2. Relate the reference positions, planes, and axes associated with the human body
3. Evaluate the skeletal considerations for movement and the different mechanics involved in
bones
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Basic Terminology   05
Biomechanics, kinesiology, anatomy, functional anatomy
linear motion, angular motion, kinematics, kinetics, statics and dynamics.
2.   Kinematic Concepts for Analyzing Human Motion   05
Linear, angular and general motion, anatomical reference position, planes
and axes, joint movement terminology, spatial reference systems, analyzing
human movement and tools for measuring kinematic quantities.
3.   Applications of Statics to Biomechanics   10
Skeletal joints, skeletal muscles, mechanics of the elbow, mechanics of the
shoulder, mechanics of the spinal column, mechanics of the hip, mechanics
of the knee and mechanics of the ankle.

report detailing the literature review, design problem formulation, analysis functional simulation and

Course Objective
This course provides the general steps used in the finite element methods and analysis of one and
two-dimensional problems. It also discusses different field problems, which relate to structural, fluid
and thermal engineering domains.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Describe the basic procedures and applications of FEA
2. Apply FEA to heat transfer and fluid flow problems in the field
3. Analyze the stiffness matrix for a bar, beam and plane elements

Course Objective
This course provides the in-depth understanding of the structured design and development
aspects of products and imparts knowledge of business and technical concerns about the
different methodologies of product development. This course also introduces the concept of
product life cycle and product data management.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1.   Identify the different stages of product development and design with modern approaches
2. Apply the knowledge of Technology Forecasting using S-Curve in product development as per
customers need
3. Compare the benchmark products, technologies and techniques for product design

Unit   Description   Duration

by evolution and innovation, factors in product design, morphology of product
design (seven phases), standardization, simplification and specialization in
product design, product life cycle and its various phases modern approaches-
concurrent design in product development, product development team and
product development planning with reference to ISO standard, new product
development process/stages, difference between product verification and
production validation.

forecasting and Technology S-curve, Kano model, Mission statement and technical
questioning. Economic analysis of product, customer needs and satisfaction,
customer population and market segmentation, gathering customer needs
information, analysis of gathered information.

selection-design evaluation, estimation of technical feasibility, concept selection
process, Pugh’s concept, selection charts, numerical concept scoring, process of
concept embodiment, system modeling, Failure Mode Effect Analysis (FMEA),
functional modeling and decomposition, fast method, subtract and operate
procedure, establishing system functionality.

Pre-requisite: Manufacturing Processes – I & II , Materials Engineering
Course Objective
This course provides comprehensive understanding and analysis of conventional metal forming
processes such as forging, rolling, extrusion, sheet metal working and also includes recently developed
forming processes.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Connect the forming processes with their defects and remedies to avoid defective products
2. Analyse the different metal forming operations like forging, rolling, blanking, coining and
extrusion
3. Summarize the advanced metal forming processes used in the industries
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Fundamentals of Metal Forming   09
Introduction of forming processes. Concept of Formability, formability limits and
formability diagram. Wire and Tube Drawing- Introduction rod and wire drawing
machines - construction and working. Preparation of stock for wire drawing. Wire
drawing dies, material and design. Heat treatment, variables in wire drawing,
Maximum reduction in wire in one pass, forces required in drawing. Multiple
drawing, defects in drawing and remedies, work hardening, lubrication in wire
drawing. Tube drawing: Methods, force calculations. Lubrication in tube drawing.
2.   Forging   07
Introduction, classification of forging processes, forging equipment- Hammers,
presses, furnaces etc. construction working capacities and selection of equipment.
Basic forging operations such as drawing, fullering edging, blocking etc.
Forgeability tests, design of forging as a product, friction in forging. Forging defects
and the remedies. New technologies: liquid metal forging, isothermal forging, draft
forging, Rotary swaging, Roll forging, lubrication in forging.
3.   Rolling of Metals   08
Scope and importance of rolling. Effect of grain direction in rolling Types of Rolling
Mills- construction and working. Deformation in rolling and determination forces
required. Process variables, redundant deformation, Roll bite and friction. Roll
flattening, Roll camber - its effect on rolling process, mill spring. Defects in rolling.
Automatic gauge control- Roll pass classification & design. Lubrication in rolling.

Mukesh Patel School of Technology Management and Engineering
4.   Sheet Metal Working   07
Sheet Metal properties, gauges and surface conditions. Various cutting and forming
operations, types of dies used, force requirement, theory of shear, methods of force
reduction, defects, lubricants used. Miscellaneous sheet metal working operations:
Metal spinning, fine blanking, coining, embossing, rubber forming, stretch forming.
Coining Embossing, Curling, Spinning and fine blanking.
5.   Extrusion   07
Extrusion types: Direct, reverse, impact, hydrostatic extrusion. Dies for extrusion,
stock penetration. Extrusion ratio of force equipment (with and without friction),
metal flow in extrusion, defects. Role of friction and lubricants. Manufacture of
seam-less tubes.
6.   Advanced Metal Forming Processes   07
Introduction to High velocity forming- principles, comparison of high velocity and
conventional forming processes. Explosive forming, Magnetic pulse forming,
electro hydraulic forming. Stretch forming, flow forming advantages, limitations
and application of the process.
Total   45

Pre-requisite: Manufacturing Processes I and II, Machine Drawing, CAD/CAM/CIM
Course Objective
The objective of the course is to introduce students to Additive Manufacturing (AM) and its
capabilities in the modern digital manufacturing industry. It is structured to familiarize students
with operating principles and applications of most prominent technologies in the field of Additive
Manufacturing.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Relate the fundamental principles of various Additive Manufacturing (AM) technologies,
material requirements and cost considerations with regards to each AM process
2. Identify critical areas where AM can be applied to create value for the entire product life-cycle
3. Apply the necessary skills in selecting the right AM process for a given application
Detailed Syllabus
Unit Description   Duration
1.   Introduction to Additive Manufacturing   04
Introduction to AM, history of AM, definition, distinction between AM, CNC &
other digital manufacturing techniques, reasons to use AM, classifications of AM
processes, design for Additive Manufacturing (DfAM), AM industry: present and
future, AM process chain, CAD and file formats for AM.
2.   Extrusion based AM processes   05
Fused deposition Modelling (FDM), history of FDM, material requirements,
workflow: material loading, liquefaction, bonding, solidification, support
generation, nozzle dynamics, applications, benefits and limitations,   post-
processing, material characterization, extrusion of: ceramics, metals, biomaterials,
composites, non-planer systems, contour crafting, concrete printing.

Stereolithography apparatus (SLA), history of SLA, material requirements,
workflow: SLA chemistry, reaction mechanism, scan patterns, applications,
benefits and limitations, other liquid polymer-based systems: solid ground curing
SGC, Microstreolithography, Digital Light Processing DLP, Continuous Liquid
Interface Production CLIP, Large-Scale Rapid Liquid Printing.
4.   Sheet Lamination AM Processes   04
Laminated Object Manufacturing (LOM), LOM of paper, polymer and composite
sheets, LOM mechanism: gluing, adhesive bonding, bond then from, from then
bond, thermal bonding,   sheet metal clamping, Ultrasonic Additive

parameters, material characterization.

characterization and selection, Selective Laser Melting (SLM): process workflow
and material requirements, powder melting mechanism, melt pool dynamics,
laser scan patterns, post-processing, powder production, handling and recycling,

Course Objective

improve product quality and process efficiency by identifying and measuring production process
variability, which, if not successfully addressed can lead to inconsistent product quality, costly
wastage, and other reliability and productivity problems.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Describe basic quality management concepts and diagnose quality problems
2. Apply Statistical Process Control (SPC) techniques as a mean to diagnose, reduce and
eliminate causes of variation
3. Create design of experiments for improving quality and increasing productivity

Pre-requisite: Fluid Mechanics, Strength of Materials and Design of Machine Elements
Course Objective
The course deals with the design and analysis of pressure vessels. The course addresses different
types of materials handling equipment and the design of belt conveyors. This course also discusses
about the design of pipelines which are the preferred mode of freight transport in many situations.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Design of pressure vessels for industrial needs
2. Choose a belt conveyor and hoisting mechanisms for different applications
3. Examine the design of pipelines for various needs
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Pressure Vessels   05
Pressure vessel construction codes, design procedure, selection of materials,
layout, elastic stress analysis, cylindrical and spherical shells, vessel components,
considerations in design.
2.   Material Handling   05
Hand trucks, Power trucks, Forklift trucks, Tractors, Parts of hoisting equipment,
hoists, winches, elevators, cranes, derricks
3.   Belt Conveyors
General applications, conveyor arrangements, characteristics of bulk materials,   10
capacities, belt widths, speeds, belt conveyor idlers, belt tension, power, drive
engineering, selection of belt.
4.   Pipelines
Friction factor, Equivalent Pipe Lengths, Hydraulic Radius, Compressible Flow,   10
Pipe Sizing, Basic Code Equations, Pipe Turns, Miter Bends, External Pressure

text:

Pre-requisite: - NA
Objective
The objective of this course is to help the students understand the principles and applications
relevant to the planning, design, and operations of manufacturing or service firms. This course
also develops an understanding about quality management practices in organizations that facilitate
organizational effectiveness.
Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Develop an understanding of manufacturing and service operations management as a
subject and outline the strategic concerns involved in operations decisions
2. Apply the principles, philosophy underpinning inventory management techniques, just-
in-time and MRP systems along with their limitations
3. Analyze the economic aspects related to production management
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Concept of Production Management   07
Meaning of production, production process system, scope of production
management, objectives of production management, functions and scopes
of production management, scope of production management, brief history
of production management, responsibilities of production manager.
2.   Productivity   04
Introduction, meaning of productivity, factors affecting on productivity,
productivity improvement, measurement of productivity.
3.   Economic Analysis   06
Factors to be considered in product design. production cost concepts;
fixed cost, variable cost, break even analysis,
P-V chart, and make-buy decision.
4.   Plant Location and Plant Layout   06
Meaning of plant layout, objective of a good plant layout, factors to be
considered in plant location, types of plant layout, process layout.
techniques of plant layout, concept of group technology, group layout.
5.   Production Planning and Control (PPC)   08
Objective of PPC, functions of PPC, capacity planning, manufacturing
resource planning and scheduling, JIT system, Kanban pull system of
scheduling, line balancing.

6.   Materials Management   07
Bill of materials, quantity planning, inventory control, economic order
quantity (EOQ), lead time, consumption rate, different ordering systems, Q
system, P system, the store’s function and ABC analysis.
7.   Quality   07
Introduction to quality control, quality management, function of quality,
quality control stages, function of inspection, statistical quality control,

text:

Teaching Scheme   Evaluation Scheme

(Hours per   (Hours per   (Hours per   Credit   Assessment (ICA)   Examinations (TEE)
week)   week)   week)   (Marks - 50)   (Marks- 100)
2   2   0   3   Marks Scaled to 50   Marks Scaled to 50
Pre-requisite: Fluid Dynamics, Heat Transfer
Course Objective
This course aims to introduce students to the major CFD theories, approaches, and methodologies
as well as provide training on the fundamental features of the CFD software ANSYS.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the students will be able to -
1.   Identify the need for modelling and simulation and to grasp its implementation
methodology
2. Analyze the cases of thermos-fluid problems
3.   Formulate a problem for its complete CFD analysis
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Introduction to CFD & Mathematical Description   05
Scope and application of CFD, methodology of CFD analysis-preprocessing,
solver, post processing. Concept of mathematical modeling, Governing
Equations in differential form. Initial and boundary value problems. Finite
Element, Finite difference and Finite Volume methods.
2.   Grid Generation and Discretization Methods   08
Structured and unstructured grids, types of grids structured grid generation,
mesh adaptation. The discretization concept, the structure of the discretization
equation, methods of deriving the discretization equations, Taylor-Series
Formulation, Variational Formulation, Method of Weighted Residuals,
Control Volume Formulation.
3.   Solution Methods of Finite Difference Equations   07
Elliptic equations – Finite difference formulations, Iterative Solution Methods,
Direct method with Gaussian Elimination; Parabolic Equations – Explicit
Schemes and Von Neumann Stability Analysis, Implicit Schemes.
4.   Numerical Modeling of Heat Conduction, Convection-diffusion   06
Steady & unsteady one-dimensional and two-dimensional conduction,
stability criterion, Steady & unsteady One-dimensional and Two-
Dimensional Convection-Diffusion.
5.   Incompressible Fluid Flow   04
Governing Equations, Stream Function-Vorticity Method, Determination of
Pressure for Viscous Flow, The SIMPLE, SIMPLER Algorithm, different
turbulence models.
Total   30

Pre-requisite: Basic Electrical and Electronics Engineering, Calculus, Engineering Mechanics,
Classical Physics
Course Objective
The objective of this course is to familiarize the learner with the electric and hybrid vehicle
architecture, technologies and fundamentals. The use of tools to design and simulate electric and
hybrid vehicles is also covered.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Explain electric and hybrid vehicle technology and its dynamics
2. Compare motors, batteries and controllers used in electric and hybrid vehicles
3. Evaluate incentives and barriers encountered in the use of EV technology
4. Simulate electric hybrid vehicle systems
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Electric and Hybrid Vehicles Introduction   04
EVs and hybrids, correlation of cost and emissions, some myth busting facts, EV
layouts and architecture, hybrid vehicle layouts.
2.   Vehicle Dynamics   06
Introduction, Forces acting on a Rolling vehicle, Power required for rolling
motion, Modeling Real-World conditions.
3.   Motors   05
Introduction, the Lorentz Force law, Coulomb’s, Biot-Savarts law, brush and
brushless motors, reluctance Motors, Faraday’s law, AC induction motors, motor
efficiency, maximum acceleration.
4.   Batteries   02
Introduction, battery fundamentals, lithium-ion batteries, battery characteristics,
electric vehicle charging.
5.   Controllers   03
Introduction, circuit elements, step-down DC controllers, step-up/down DC
controllers, AC controllers.
6.   Incentives and Barriers   04
Introduction, national incentives, state incentives, FAME-I, FAME-II, e-AMRIT.
Barriers to development of EV infrastructure in India.

Teaching Scheme   Evaluation Scheme

(Hours per (Hours per   (Hours per   Credit   Assessment (ICA)   Examinations (TEE)

2   2   0   3   Marks Scaled to 50   Marks Scaled to 50
Pre-requisite: Engineering Mechanics, Fluid Mechanics and Strength of Materials
Course Objective
This course introduces the basic concepts of vibrations and discusses free vibration of an undamped
single-degree of-freedom system. This course also deals with two-degree-of-freedom systems, which
require two independent coordinates to describe their motion. The modeling of continuous
systems as multidegree-of-freedom systems is also presented in this course.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Derive the equation of motion of a single-degree-of-freedom system
2. Solve two-degree-of-freedom free- and forced-vibration problems
3. Formulate the equations of motion of multidegree-of-freedom systems
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Fundamentals of Vibration   07
Basic Concepts of Vibration, Classification of Vibration, Vibration Analysis
Procedure, Spring Elements, Mass or Inertia Elements, Damping Elements,
Harmonic Motion, Harmonic Analysis
2.   Single-Degree-of-Freedom Systems   08
Free Vibration of an Undamped Translational System, Free Vibration of an
Undamped Torsional System, Free Vibration with Viscous Damping, Free
Vibration with Coulomb Damping.
3.   Two-Degree-of-Freedom Systems   06
Equations of Motion for Forced Vibration, Free Vibration Analysis of an
Undamped System, Torsional System, Forced-Vibration Analysis.
4.   Multidegree-of-Freedom Systems   09
Modeling of Continuous Systems as Multi degree of Freedom Systems, Equations
of Motion, Influence Coefficients, Generalized Coordinates and Generalized
Forces, Lagrange s Equations, Equations of Motion of Undamped Systems in
Matrix Form, Eigenvalue Problem
Total   30
Text Books
1. S. S. Rao, Mechanical Vibration, Addison Wesley, 2004.
2. Michel Géradin and Daniel J. Rixen, Mechanical Vibrations Theory and Application to Structural
Dynamics, John Wiley & Sons, 2015.

Pre-requisite: Nil
Course Objective
The objective of this course is to enable the student to understand and analyze managerial and
engineering problems and to use the resources such as capitals, materials, productions, controlling,
directing, staffing, and machines more effectively.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Formulate and obtain the optimal solution for Linear Programming problems.
2. Determine the optimal solution for Assignment and Transportation problems.
3. Propose the best strategy using game theory and choose the appropriate queuing model for
a given practical application.
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Introduction to Operations Research   10
Introduction, Structure of the mathematical Model, Limitations of Operations
research
Linear Programming Models
Introduction, Mathematical formulation of LPP, Simplex Method, Penalty cost
method or Big M method, Two Phase Method, Concept of Initialization, Iteration
and Termination in LPP, Primal –Dual construction, Sensitivity Analysis, manual
solution of problems involving up to three iterations.
2.   Transportation Model   05
Introduction, Finding basic feasible solution of Transportation by- Northwest
corner rule, Least cost Method and Vogel’s approximation method. Optimality
test using Stepping Stone Method and Modified distribution method (MODI
method or U-V method).
3. Assignment and Sequencing Models   05
Introduction, Concept of Degeneracy. Minimizations, Maximization model,
conditional assignment (Hungarian Method). Processing of n jobs through two
machines and three machines, Graphical method of Two jobs through M
machines.
4. Game Theory   05
Limited to two person zero sum games; dominance principle, saddle point, pure
and mixed strategies, graphical and analytical methods; LP model formulation.

Course Objective

strength and stiffness of the aircraft. The course investigates the stresses and displacements
in thin-walled open and single-cell closed section beams produced by bending loads for an
aircraft.
Course Outcomes

1. Categorize the structural components of aircraft
2. Estimate the airworthiness of an aircraft and its airframe loads
3. Analyze aircraft components and its structural idealization

Course: Gender Communication   Code: 701BS0I001
Teaching Scheme   Evaluation Scheme

(Hours   (Hours per   (Hours per   Credit   Assessment (ICA)   (TEE)
per week)   week)   week)   (Marks - 50)   (Marks - 100)
3   0   0   3   Marks Scaled to 50   Marks Scaled to 50
Pre-requisite: NA
Course Objective
The course introduces students to some key biological aspects of genders and aims to expose them to the
interactions between men and women. It further provides an insight to the process of socialization of gender
and its intersection with class, race, ethnicity and caste.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to-
1. Classify basic dimensions of the biological, sociological, and psychological aspects of gender
2. Examine important issues related to gender in contemporary India
3. Identify how gender discrimination works in our society, so we can work and live together as equals
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Understanding Gender and Related Concepts   03
Distinguishing between Gender and Sex, Androcentrism, Femininity and Masculinity,
Heterosexism, Essentialism, Feminism, Patriarchy, sexuality and stereotype.
2.   Feminist Theory and Feminist Movements
Introduction, Liberal Feminism, Radical Feminism, Marxist Socialist Feminism,
Postmodern Feminism, Poststructuralist theory and Queer theory, Transgender and   06
Intersectionality, Ecofeminism. The First, Second and Third Wave of Feminism,
Postcolonial Feminism and Feminist movements in India.
3.   Social Stratification and Gender
Introduction, Ethnicity and Gender, Stereotyping and the Intersection of Gender and
Ethnicity, Class System: Karl Marx and Max Weber, Culture and understanding of Class   09
and Gender, Race and Gender as forms of Social Stratification, Race and Gender as Social

Course Objective
This course focusses on the application of classical mechanics to various biological problems by
combining the fields of biology and physiology. This course is concerned with the application of
principles of mechanics to the conceptualization, design, development and analysis of equipment
and systems as applied to human body.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Correlate mechanics, biomechanics and kinesiology and differentiate between their uses in the
analysis of human movement
2. Relate the reference positions, planes, and axes associated with the human body
3. Evaluate the skeletal considerations for movement and the different mechanics involved in
bones

linear motion, angular motion, kinematics, kinetics, statics and dynamics.

and axes, joint movement terminology, spatial reference systems, analyzing
human movement and tools for measuring kinematic quantities.

Skeletal joints, skeletal muscles, mechanics of the elbow, mechanics of the
shoulder, mechanics of the spinal column, mechanics of the hip, mechanics
of the knee and mechanics of the ankle.

bone, bone formation, strength and stiffness of bone, loads applied to bone,
stress fractures, articular cartilage, fibrocartilage and ligaments.

Outcomes:

concurrent design and quality function deployment, product

 To introduce duct design methods.

 Know the properties of refrigerants and binary mixtures and understand the

 Represent different air-conditioning processes on psychrometric chart and design

prominent technologies in the field of Additive Manufacturing.
 To explore the Design for Additive Manufacturing capabilities of each AM

technologies, material requirements and cost considerations with regards to each
AM process.
 Identify critical areas where AM can be applied to create value for the entire

Wave nature of Matter: De Broglie’s hypothesis, Davisson-Germer

Wave Packets and Uncertainty Principle: General statement of
Heisenberg’s Uncertainty Principle, Energy-Time and Position-
momentum uncertainty relation and its applications

Need for clean energy, different methods for obtaining clean energy
viz. nuclear energy (including basics of nuclear physics like fission
and fusion etc.) solar cells (including conventional and Nano
material based solar cells), hydrogen fuels and wind mills.
Advantagi itations of each method.
